clauses.normalized_text: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.
clauses.raw_text: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.
clauses.raw_text: TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.

clauses.normalized_text: This document updates RFCs 5705 and 6066, and obsoletes RFCs 5077, 5246, and 6961.
clauses.raw_text: This document updates RFCs 5705 and 6066, and obsoletes RFCs 5077, 5246, and 6961.

clauses.normalized_text: This document also specifies new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations.
clauses.raw_text: This document also specifies new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations.

clauses.normalized_text: The primary goal of TLS is to provide a secure channel between two communicating peers; the only requirement from the underlying transport is a reliable, in-order data stream.
clauses.raw_text: The primary goal of TLS is to provide a secure channel between two communicating peers; the only requirement from the underlying transport is a reliable, in-order data stream.

clauses.normalized_text: Specifically, the secure channel should provide the following properties:
clauses.raw_text: Specifically, the secure channel should provide the following properties:

clauses.normalized_text: Authentication: The server side of the channel is always authenticated; the client side is optionally authenticated.
clauses.raw_text: - Authentication: The server side of the channel is always authenticated; the client side is optionally authenticated.

clauses.normalized_text: Authentication can happen via asymmetric cryptography (e.g., RSA [RSA], the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) [ECDSA], or the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) [RFC8032]) or a symmetric pre-shared key (PSK).
clauses.raw_text: Authentication can happen via asymmetric cryptography (e.g., RSA [RSA], the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) [ECDSA], or the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) [RFC8032]) or a symmetric pre-shared key (PSK).

clauses.normalized_text: Confidentiality: Data sent over the channel after establishment is only visible to the endpoints.
clauses.raw_text: - Confidentiality: Data sent over the channel after establishment is only visible to the endpoints.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS does not hide the length of the data it transmits, though endpoints are able to pad TLS records in order to obscure lengths and improve protection against traffic analysis techniques.
clauses.raw_text: TLS does not hide the length of the data it transmits, though endpoints are able to pad TLS records in order to obscure lengths and improve protection against traffic analysis techniques.

clauses.normalized_text: Integrity: Data sent over the channel after establishment cannot be modified by attackers without detection.
clauses.raw_text: - Integrity: Data sent over the channel after establishment cannot be modified by attackers without detection.

clauses.normalized_text: These properties should be true even in the face of an attacker who has complete control of the network, as described in [RFC3552].
clauses.raw_text: These properties should be true even in the face of an attacker who has complete control of the network, as described in [RFC3552].

clauses.normalized_text: See Appendix E for a more complete statement of the relevant security properties.
clauses.raw_text: See Appendix E for a more complete statement of the relevant security properties.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS consists of two primary components:
clauses.raw_text: TLS consists of two primary components:

clauses.normalized_text: A handshake protocol (Section 4) that authenticates the communicating parties, negotiates cryptographic modes and parameters, and establishes shared keying material.
clauses.raw_text: - A handshake protocol (Section 4) that authenticates the communicating parties, negotiates cryptographic modes and parameters, and establishes shared keying material.

clauses.normalized_text: The handshake protocol is designed to resist tampering; an active attacker should not be able to force the peers to negotiate different parameters than they would if the connection were not under attack.
clauses.raw_text: The handshake protocol is designed to resist tampering; an active attacker should not be able to force the peers to negotiate different parameters than they would if the connection were not under attack.

clauses.normalized_text: A record protocol (Section 5) that uses the parameters established by the handshake protocol to protect traffic between the communicating peers.
clauses.raw_text: - A record protocol (Section 5) that uses the parameters established by the handshake protocol to protect traffic between the communicating peers.

clauses.normalized_text: The record protocol divides traffic up into a series of records, each of which is independently protected using the traffic keys.
clauses.raw_text: The record protocol divides traffic up into a series of records, each of which is independently protected using the traffic keys.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS is application protocol independent; higher-level protocols can layer on top of TLS transparently.
clauses.raw_text: TLS is application protocol independent; higher-level protocols can layer on top of TLS transparently.

clauses.normalized_text: The TLS standard, however, does not specify how protocols add security with TLS; how to initiate TLS handshaking and how to interpret the authentication certificates exchanged are left to the judgment of the designers and implementors of protocols that run on top of TLS.
clauses.raw_text: The TLS standard, however, does not specify how protocols add security with TLS; how to initiate TLS handshaking and how to interpret the authentication certificates exchanged are left to the judgment of the designers and implementors of protocols that run on top of TLS.

clauses.normalized_text: This document defines TLS version 1.3.
clauses.raw_text: This document defines TLS version 1.3.

clauses.normalized_text: While TLS 1.3 is not directly compatible with previous versions, all versions of TLS incorporate a versioning mechanism which allows clients and servers to interoperably negotiate a common version if one is supported by both peers.
clauses.raw_text: While TLS 1.3 is not directly compatible with previous versions, all versions of TLS incorporate a versioning mechanism which allows clients and servers to interoperably negotiate a common version if one is supported by both peers.

clauses.normalized_text: This document supersedes and obsoletes previous versions of TLS, including version 1.2 [RFC5246].
clauses.raw_text: This document supersedes and obsoletes previous versions of TLS, including version 1.2 [RFC5246].

clauses.normalized_text: It also obsoletes the TLS ticket mechanism defined in [RFC5077] and replaces it with the mechanism defined in Section 2.2.
clauses.raw_text: It also obsoletes the TLS ticket mechanism defined in [RFC5077] and replaces it with the mechanism defined in Section 2.2.

clauses.normalized_text: Because TLS 1.3 changes the way keys are derived, it updates [RFC5705] as described in Section 7.5.
clauses.raw_text: Because TLS 1.3 changes the way keys are derived, it updates [RFC5705] as described in Section 7.5.

clauses.normalized_text: It also changes how Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) messages are carried and therefore updates [RFC6066] and obsoletes [RFC6961] as described in Section 4.4.2.1.
clauses.raw_text: It also changes how Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) messages are carried and therefore updates [RFC6066] and obsoletes [RFC6961] as described in Section 4.4.2.1.

clauses.raw_text: The following terms are used:

clauses.normalized_text: client: The endpoint initiating the TLS connection.

clauses.raw_text: connection: A transport-layer connection between two endpoints.

clauses.normalized_text: endpoint: Either the client or server of the connection.
clauses.raw_text: endpoint: Either the client or server of the connection.

clauses.normalized_text: handshake: An initial negotiation between client and server that establishes the parameters of their subsequent interactions within TLS.
clauses.raw_text: handshake: An initial negotiation between client and server that establishes the parameters of their subsequent interactions within TLS.

clauses.normalized_text: peer: An endpoint.
clauses.raw_text: peer: An endpoint.

clauses.normalized_text: When discussing a particular endpoint, "peer" refers to the endpoint that is not the primary subject of discussion.
clauses.raw_text: When discussing a particular endpoint, "peer" refers to the endpoint that is not the primary subject of discussion.

clauses.normalized_text: receiver: An endpoint that is receiving records.
clauses.raw_text: receiver: An endpoint that is receiving records.

clauses.normalized_text: sender: An endpoint that is transmitting records.
clauses.raw_text: sender: An endpoint that is transmitting records.

clauses.normalized_text: server: The endpoint that did not initiate the TLS connection.
clauses.raw_text: server: The endpoint that did not initiate the TLS connection.

clauses.normalized_text: The following is a list of the major functional differences between TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
clauses.raw_text: The following is a list of the major functional differences between TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

clauses.normalized_text: It is not intended to be exhaustive, and there are many minor differences.
clauses.raw_text: It is not intended to be exhaustive, and there are many minor differences.

clauses.normalized_text: The list of supported symmetric encryption algorithms has been pruned of all algorithms that are considered legacy.
clauses.raw_text: - The list of supported symmetric encryption algorithms has been pruned of all algorithms that are considered legacy.

clauses.normalized_text: Those that remain are all Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms.
clauses.raw_text: Those that remain are all Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms.

clauses.normalized_text: The cipher suite concept has been changed to separate the authentication and key exchange mechanisms from the record protection algorithm (including secret key length) and a hash to be used with both the key derivation function and handshake message authentication code (MAC).
clauses.raw_text: The cipher suite concept has been changed to separate the authentication and key exchange mechanisms from the record protection algorithm (including secret key length) and a hash to be used with both the key derivation function and handshake message authentication code (MAC).

clauses.normalized_text: A zero round-trip time (0-RTT) mode was added, saving a round trip at connection setup for some application data, at the cost of certain security properties.
clauses.raw_text: - A zero round-trip time (0-RTT) mode was added, saving a round trip at connection setup for some application data, at the cost of certain security properties.

clauses.normalized_text: Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites have been removed; all public-key based key exchange mechanisms now provide forward secrecy.
clauses.raw_text: - Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites have been removed; all public-key based key exchange mechanisms now provide forward secrecy.

clauses.normalized_text: All handshake messages after the ServerHello are now encrypted.
clauses.raw_text: - All handshake messages after the ServerHello are now encrypted.

clauses.normalized_text: The newly introduced EncryptedExtensions message allows various extensions previously sent in the clear in the ServerHello to also enjoy confidentiality protection.
clauses.raw_text: The newly introduced EncryptedExtensions message allows various extensions previously sent in the clear in the ServerHello to also enjoy confidentiality protection.

clauses.normalized_text: The key derivation functions have been redesigned.
clauses.raw_text: - The key derivation functions have been redesigned.

clauses.normalized_text: The new design allows easier analysis by cryptographers due to their improved key separation properties.
clauses.raw_text: The new design allows easier analysis by cryptographers due to their improved key separation properties.

clauses.normalized_text: The HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF) is used as an underlying primitive.
clauses.raw_text: The HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF) is used as an underlying primitive.

clauses.normalized_text: The handshake state machine has been significantly restructured to be more consistent and to remove superfluous messages such as ChangeCipherSpec (except when needed for middlebox compatibility).
clauses.raw_text: - The handshake state machine has been significantly restructured to be more consistent and to remove superfluous messages such as ChangeCipherSpec (except when needed for middlebox compatibility).

clauses.normalized_text: Elliptic curve algorithms are now in the base spec, and new signature algorithms, such as EdDSA, are included.
clauses.raw_text: - Elliptic curve algorithms are now in the base spec, and new signature algorithms, such as EdDSA, are included.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS 1.3 removed point format negotiation in favor of a single point format for each curve.
clauses.raw_text: TLS 1.3 removed point format negotiation in favor of a single point format for each curve.

clauses.normalized_text: Other cryptographic improvements were made, including changing the RSA padding to use the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS), and the removal of compression, the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), and custom Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) groups.
clauses.raw_text: - Other cryptographic improvements were made, including changing the RSA padding to use the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS), and the removal of compression, the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), and custom Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) groups.

clauses.normalized_text: The TLS 1.2 version negotiation mechanism has been deprecated in favor of a version list in an extension.
clauses.raw_text: - The TLS 1.2 version negotiation mechanism has been deprecated in favor of a version list in an extension.

clauses.normalized_text: This increases compatibility with existing servers that incorrectly implemented version negotiation.
clauses.raw_text: This increases compatibility with existing servers that incorrectly implemented version negotiation.

clauses.normalized_text: Session resumption with and without server-side state as well as the PSK-based cipher suites of earlier TLS versions have been replaced by a single new PSK exchange.
clauses.raw_text: - Session resumption with and without server-side state as well as the PSK-based cipher suites of earlier TLS versions have been replaced by a single new PSK exchange.

clauses.normalized_text: References have been updated to point to the updated versions of RFCs, as appropriate (e.g., RFC 5280 rather than RFC 3280).
clauses.raw_text: - References have been updated to point to the updated versions of RFCs, as appropriate (e.g., RFC 5280 rather than RFC 3280).

clauses.normalized_text: This document defines several changes that optionally affect implementations of TLS 1.2, including those which do not also support TLS 1.3:
clauses.raw_text: This document defines several changes that optionally affect implementations of TLS 1.2, including those which do not also support TLS 1.3:

clauses.normalized_text: A version downgrade protection mechanism is described in Section 4.1.3.
clauses.raw_text: - A version downgrade protection mechanism is described in Section 4.1.3.

clauses.normalized_text: RSASSA-PSS signature schemes are defined in Section 4.2.3.
clauses.raw_text: - RSASSA-PSS signature schemes are defined in Section 4.2.3.

clauses.normalized_text: The "supported_versions" ClientHello extension can be used to negotiate the version of TLS to use, in preference to the legacy_version field of the ClientHello.
clauses.raw_text: - The "supported_versions" ClientHello extension can be used to negotiate the version of TLS to use, in preference to the legacy_version field of the ClientHello.

clauses.normalized_text: The "signature_algorithms_cert" extension allows a client to indicate which signature algorithms it can validate in X.509 certificates.
clauses.raw_text: - The "signature_algorithms_cert" extension allows a client to indicate which signature algorithms it can validate in X.509 certificates.

clauses.normalized_text: Additionally, this document clarifies some compliance requirements for earlier versions of TLS; see Section 9.3.
clauses.raw_text: Additionally, this document clarifies some compliance requirements for earlier versions of TLS; see Section 9.3.

clauses.normalized_text: The cryptographic parameters used by the secure channel are produced by the TLS handshake protocol.
clauses.raw_text: The cryptographic parameters used by the secure channel are produced by the TLS handshake protocol.

clauses.normalized_text: This sub-protocol of TLS is used by the client and server when first communicating with each other.
clauses.raw_text: This sub-protocol of TLS is used by the client and server when first communicating with each other.

clauses.normalized_text: The handshake protocol allows peers to negotiate a protocol version, select cryptographic algorithms, optionally authenticate each other, and establish shared secret keying material.
clauses.raw_text: The handshake protocol allows peers to negotiate a protocol version, select cryptographic algorithms, optionally authenticate each other, and establish shared secret keying material.

clauses.normalized_text: Once the handshake is complete, the peers use the established keys to protect the application-layer traffic.
clauses.raw_text: Once the handshake is complete, the peers use the established keys to protect the application-layer traffic.

clauses.normalized_text: A failure of the handshake or other protocol error triggers the termination of the connection, optionally preceded by an alert message (Section 6).
clauses.raw_text: A failure of the handshake or other protocol error triggers the termination of the connection, optionally preceded by an alert message (Section 6).

clauses.normalized_text: The handshake can be thought of as having three phases (indicated in the diagram above):
clauses.raw_text: The handshake can be thought of as having three phases (indicated in the diagram above):

clauses.normalized_text: Key Exchange: Establish shared keying material and select the cryptographic parameters.
clauses.raw_text: - Key Exchange: Establish shared keying material and select the cryptographic parameters.

clauses.normalized_text: Everything after this phase is encrypted.
clauses.raw_text: Everything after this phase is encrypted.

clauses.normalized_text: Server Parameters: Establish other handshake parameters (whether the client is authenticated, application-layer protocol support, etc.).
clauses.raw_text: - Server Parameters: Establish other handshake parameters (whether the client is authenticated, application-layer protocol support, etc.).

clauses.normalized_text: Authentication: Authenticate the server (and, optionally, the client) and provide key confirmation and handshake integrity.
clauses.raw_text: - Authentication: Authenticate the server (and, optionally, the client) and provide key confirmation and handshake integrity.

clauses.normalized_text: In the Key Exchange phase, the client sends the ClientHello (Section 4.1.2) message, which contains a random nonce (ClientHello.random); its offered protocol versions; a list of symmetric cipher/HKDF hash pairs; either a set of Diffie-Hellman key shares (in the "key_share" (Section 4.2.8) extension), a set of pre-shared key labels (in the "pre_shared_key" (Section 4.2.11) extension), or both; and potentially additional extensions.
clauses.raw_text: In the Key Exchange phase, the client sends the ClientHello (Section 4.1.2) message, which contains a random nonce (ClientHello.random); its offered protocol versions; a list of symmetric cipher/HKDF hash pairs; either a set of Diffie-Hellman key shares (in the "key_share" (Section 4.2.8) extension), a set of pre-shared key labels (in the "pre_shared_key" (Section 4.2.11) extension), or both; and potentially additional extensions.

clauses.normalized_text: Additional fields and/or messages may also be present for middlebox compatibility.
clauses.raw_text: Additional fields and/or messages may also be present for middlebox compatibility.

clauses.normalized_text: The server processes the ClientHello and determines the appropriate cryptographic parameters for the connection.
clauses.raw_text: The server processes the ClientHello and determines the appropriate cryptographic parameters for the connection.

clauses.normalized_text: It then responds with its own ServerHello (Section 4.1.3), which indicates the negotiated connection parameters.
clauses.raw_text: It then responds with its own ServerHello (Section 4.1.3), which indicates the negotiated connection parameters.

clauses.normalized_text: The combination of the ClientHello and the ServerHello determines the shared keys.
clauses.raw_text: The combination of the ClientHello and the ServerHello determines the shared keys.

clauses.normalized_text: If (EC)DHE key establishment is in use, then the ServerHello contains a "key_share" extension with the server's ephemeral Diffie-Hellman share; the server's share MUST be in the same group as one of the client's shares.
clauses.raw_text: If (EC)DHE key establishment is in use, then the ServerHello contains a "key_share" extension with the server's ephemeral Diffie-Hellman share; the server's share MUST be in the same group as one of the client's shares.

clauses.normalized_text: If PSK key establishment is in use, then the ServerHello contains a "pre_shared_key" extension indicating which of the client's offered PSKs was selected.
clauses.raw_text: If PSK key establishment is in use, then the ServerHello contains a "pre_shared_key" extension indicating which of the client's offered PSKs was selected.

clauses.normalized_text: Note that implementations can use (EC)DHE and PSK together, in which case both extensions will be supplied.
clauses.raw_text: Note that implementations can use (EC)DHE and PSK together, in which case both extensions will be supplied.

clauses.raw_text: The server then sends two messages to establish the Server Parameters:

clauses.normalized_text: EncryptedExtensions: responses to ClientHello extensions that are not required to determine the cryptographic parameters, other than those that are specific to individual certificates.

clauses.raw_text: CertificateVerify: A signature over the entire handshake using the private key corresponding to the public key in the Certificate message.

clauses.normalized_text: This message is omitted if the endpoint is not authenticating via a certificate.

clauses.normalized_text: Finished: A MAC (Message Authentication Code) over the entire handshake.
clauses.raw_text: Finished: A MAC (Message Authentication Code) over the entire handshake.

clauses.normalized_text: This message provides key confirmation, binds the endpoint's identity to the exchanged keys, and in PSK mode also authenticates the handshake.

clauses.normalized_text: Upon receiving the server's messages, the client responds with its Authentication messages, namely Certificate and CertificateVerify (if requested), and Finished.

clauses.normalized_text: At this point, the handshake is complete, and the client and server derive the keying material required by the record layer to exchange application-layer data protected through authenticated encryption.

clauses.normalized_text: This section describes invariants that TLS endpoints and middleboxes MUST follow.
clauses.raw_text: This section describes invariants that TLS endpoints and middleboxes MUST follow.

clauses.normalized_text: It also applies to earlier versions of TLS.
clauses.raw_text: It also applies to earlier versions of TLS.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS is designed to be securely and compatibly extensible.
clauses.raw_text: TLS is designed to be securely and compatibly extensible.

clauses.normalized_text: Newer clients or servers, when communicating with newer peers, should negotiate the most preferred common parameters.
clauses.raw_text: Newer clients or servers, when communicating with newer peers, should negotiate the most preferred common parameters.

clauses.normalized_text: The TLS handshake provides downgrade protection: Middleboxes passing traffic between a newer client and newer server without terminating TLS should be unable to influence the handshake (see Appendix E.1).
clauses.raw_text: The TLS handshake provides downgrade protection: Middleboxes passing traffic between a newer client and newer server without terminating TLS should be unable to influence the handshake (see Appendix E.1).

clauses.normalized_text: At the same time, deployments update at different rates, so a newer client or server MAY continue to support older parameters, which would allow it to interoperate with older endpoints.
clauses.raw_text: At the same time, deployments update at different rates, so a newer client or server MAY continue to support older parameters, which would allow it to interoperate with older endpoints.

clauses.normalized_text: For this to work, implementations MUST correctly handle extensible fields:
clauses.raw_text: For this to work, implementations MUST correctly handle extensible fields:

clauses.normalized_text: A client sending a ClientHello MUST support all parameters advertised in it.
clauses.raw_text: - A client sending a ClientHello MUST support all parameters advertised in it.

clauses.normalized_text: Otherwise, the server may fail to interoperate by selecting one of those parameters.
clauses.raw_text: Otherwise, the server may fail to interoperate by selecting one of those parameters.

clauses.normalized_text: A server receiving a ClientHello MUST correctly ignore all unrecognized cipher suites, extensions, and other parameters.
clauses.raw_text: - A server receiving a ClientHello MUST correctly ignore all unrecognized cipher suites, extensions, and other parameters.

clauses.normalized_text: Otherwise, it may fail to interoperate with newer clients.
clauses.raw_text: Otherwise, it may fail to interoperate with newer clients.

clauses.normalized_text: In TLS 1.3, a client receiving a CertificateRequest or NewSessionTicket MUST also ignore all unrecognized extensions.
clauses.raw_text: In TLS 1.3, a client receiving a CertificateRequest or NewSessionTicket MUST also ignore all unrecognized extensions.

clauses.normalized_text: A middlebox which terminates a TLS connection MUST behave as a compliant TLS server (to the original client), including having a certificate which the client is willing to accept, and also as a compliant TLS client (to the original server), including verifying the original server's certificate.
clauses.raw_text: - A middlebox which terminates a TLS connection MUST behave as a compliant TLS server (to the original client), including having a certificate which the client is willing to accept, and also as a compliant TLS client (to the original server), including verifying the original server's certificate.

clauses.normalized_text: In particular, it MUST generate its own ClientHello containing only parameters it understands, and it MUST generate a fresh ServerHello random value, rather than forwarding the endpoint's value.
clauses.raw_text: In particular, it MUST generate its own ClientHello containing only parameters it understands, and it MUST generate a fresh ServerHello random value, rather than forwarding the endpoint's value.

clauses.normalized_text: Note that TLS's protocol requirements and security analysis only apply to the two connections separately.
clauses.raw_text: Note that TLS's protocol requirements and security analysis only apply to the two connections separately.

clauses.normalized_text: Safely deploying a TLS terminator requires additional security considerations which are beyond the scope of this document.
clauses.raw_text: Safely deploying a TLS terminator requires additional security considerations which are beyond the scope of this document.

clauses.normalized_text: A middlebox which forwards ClientHello parameters it does not understand MUST NOT process any messages beyond that ClientHello.
clauses.raw_text: - A middlebox which forwards ClientHello parameters it does not understand MUST NOT process any messages beyond that ClientHello.

clauses.normalized_text: It MUST forward all subsequent traffic unmodified.
clauses.raw_text: It MUST forward all subsequent traffic unmodified.

clauses.normalized_text: Otherwise, it may fail to interoperate with newer clients and servers.
clauses.raw_text: Otherwise, it may fail to interoperate with newer clients and servers.

clauses.normalized_text: Forwarded ClientHellos may contain advertisements for features not supported by the middlebox, so the response may include future TLS additions the middlebox does not recognize.
clauses.raw_text: Forwarded ClientHellos may contain advertisements for features not supported by the middlebox, so the response may include future TLS additions the middlebox does not recognize.

clauses.normalized_text: These additions MAY change any message beyond the ClientHello arbitrarily.
clauses.raw_text: These additions MAY change any message beyond the ClientHello arbitrarily.

clauses.normalized_text: In particular, the values sent in the ServerHello might change, the ServerHello format might change, and the TLSCiphertext format might change.
clauses.raw_text: In particular, the values sent in the ServerHello might change, the ServerHello format might change, and the TLSCiphertext format might change.

clauses.normalized_text: The design of TLS 1.3 was constrained by widely deployed non-compliant TLS middleboxes (see Appendix D.4); however, it does not relax the invariants.
clauses.raw_text: The design of TLS 1.3 was constrained by widely deployed non-compliant TLS middleboxes (see Appendix D.4); however, it does not relax the invariants.

clauses.normalized_text: Those middleboxes continue to be non-compliant.
clauses.raw_text: Those middleboxes continue to be non-compliant.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS requires a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG).
clauses.raw_text: TLS requires a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG).

clauses.normalized_text: In most cases, the operating system provides an appropriate facility such as /dev/urandom, which should be used absent other (e.g., performance) concerns.

clauses.raw_text: It is RECOMMENDED to use an existing CSPRNG implementation in preference to crafting a new one.

clauses.normalized_text: Many adequate cryptographic libraries are already available under favorable license terms.

clauses.normalized_text: Should those prove unsatisfactory, [RFC4086] provides guidance on the generation of random values.

clauses.normalized_text: TLS uses random values (1) in public protocol fields such as the public Random values in the ClientHello and ServerHello and (2) to generate keying material.
clauses.raw_text: TLS uses random values (1) in public protocol fields such as the public Random values in the ClientHello and ServerHello and (2) to generate keying material.

clauses.normalized_text: With a properly functioning CSPRNG, this does not present a security problem, as it is not feasible to determine the CSPRNG state from its output.
clauses.raw_text: With a properly functioning CSPRNG, this does not present a security problem, as it is not feasible to determine the CSPRNG state from its output.

clauses.normalized_text: However, with a broken CSPRNG, it may be possible for an attacker to use the public output to determine the CSPRNG internal state and thereby predict the keying material, as documented in [CHECKOWAY].
clauses.raw_text: However, with a broken CSPRNG, it may be possible for an attacker to use the public output to determine the CSPRNG internal state and thereby predict the keying material, as documented in [CHECKOWAY].

clauses.normalized_text: Implementations can provide extra security against this form of attack by using separate CSPRNGs to generate public and private values.
clauses.raw_text: Implementations can provide extra security against this form of attack by using separate CSPRNGs to generate public and private values.
